chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Muawiya ibn Wahb, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him, 'A man from your mawali, from their righteous ones, complained to me about what he faces from sleep, and said, 'I intend to stand for prayer at night, but sleep overcomes me until morning, and sometimes I make up my prayers for the month consecutively, and for two months I bear the heaviness of it.' So he said, 'A delight of the eye for him, by Allah.'
He said, 'And he did not permit him to pray in the first part of the night, and said, 'Making up the prayers during the day is superior.'

I said, 'But among our women are young girls who love goodness and its people, and are eager for prayer, but sleep overcomes them so that sometimes they make it up, and sometimes they are too weak to make it up, and they are strong upon it in the first part of the night.' So he permitted them to pray in the first part of the night when they were too weak and missed making up the prayers.

key_terms.أَوَّلُ اللَّيْلِ: The first part of the night

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on making up missed night prayers due to sleep?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes a general principle that making up voluntary night prayers during the day is superior, reflecting the scholarly view that consistency in the prescribed time is ideal. However, he introduces a pragmatic exception for young women (or those with similar physical constraints) who, despite their eagerness, are overcome by sleep early in the night, thereby permitting them to pray later when they are too weak to maintain vigilance. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential balance between spiritual aspiration (*hawas*) and physical capacity (*qudra*), emphasizing that divine mercy accommodates human frailty without diminishing the value of the act.
